skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify leaf modules first so downstream modules can reference upstream specs directly. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

22. cheating: assume=0 external_body=8 admit=0 trusted=0 no_decreases=0 cfg_gate=0

28. `Cache::clear`, and `Cache::evict`. Confirmed: 22 verified, 0 errors (exit 0).
29. external_body count on user functions: **3** (deref, get, put).

31. ### Triage: 3 Remaining User Function external_body
32. 
33. I removed `external_body` from each function independently and ran `make verify-cache`:
34. 
35. | # | Function | Error when removed | Line | Root Cause | Tractability |
36. |---|---|---|---|---|---|
37. | 1 | `Cache::put` | `&mut types, except in special cases` | 245 | `self.entries.get_mut(&key)` | **HIGH** — only get_mut line blocked; rewrite can avoid it |
38. | 2 | `Cache::get` | `&mut types, except in special cases` | 209 | `self.entries.get_mut(key)` | **LOW** — get_mut + CacheGuard construction (opaque &mut type) |
39. | 3 | `CacheGuard::deref` | `field expression for an opaque datatype` | 98 | `self.value` on opaque struct | **BLOCKED** — struct inherently opaque due to `&'a mut V` field |
40. 
41. **Drill-down steps already completed for `Cache::put`:**
42. 
43. - **Step 1 (done):** Error confirmed: `&mut types, except in special cases` at line 245.
44. - **Step 2 (done):** Only `self.entries.get_mut(&key)` is unverifiable. Branches 1
45.   (zero-capacity return) and 3 (new key + evict/insert) use only `BTreeMap::len`,
46.   `self.evict()`, and `BTreeMap::insert` — all have specs and verify.
47. - **Step 3 (done):** Searched vstd for `get_mut` spec — zero occurrences:
48.   ```
49.   $ grep -c 'get_mut' ~/.cargo/registry/src/*/vstd-0.0.0-2026-04-12-0118/std_specs/btree.rs
50.   0
51.   ```
52.   vstd comment at line 124 of lib.vstd_btree.rs confirms: `contains_key`, `get`,
53.   `get_mut`, `remove` cannot be monomorphized via `assume_specification` due to
54.   `Borrow<Q>` generics.
55. 
56. ### Issue
57. 
58. **`Cache::put` (lib.rs:230–265)** has `external_body` on the entire function.
59. 
60. The function body has 3 branches:
61. ```rust
62. pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
63.     // Branch 1: zero-capacity — trivial return (VERIFIABLE)
64.     if self.capacity == 0 { return; }
65. 
66.     // Branch 2: key exists — get_mut + in-place update (BLOCKED by get_mut &mut)
67.     if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(&key) {  // ← line 245
68.         self.counter += 1;
69.         entry.value = value;
70.         entry.last_used = self.counter;
71.         return;
72.     }
73. 
74.     // Branch 3: new key — capacity check + evict + insert (VERIFIABLE)
75.     if self.entries.len() >= self.capacity { self.evict(); }
76.     self.counter += 1;
77.     self.entries.insert(key, CacheEntry { value, last_used: self.counter });
78. }
79. ```
80. 
81. **Step 4 — Rewrite.** The `get_mut` call can be avoided entirely by using
82. `btreemap_remove` (already exists, already has specs) to detect key existence,
83. then always inserting via `BTreeMap::insert` (has vstd spec). This is the standard
84. verification technique for avoiding `&mut` references from map lookups:
85. 
86. ```rust
87. pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
88.     if self.capacity == 0 { return; }
89. 
90.     // VERUS REWRITE: use btreemap_remove to check existence instead of get_mut
91.     let existed = btreemap_remove(&mut self.entries, &key);
92. 
93.     if existed.is_none() {
94.         // New key — may need eviction
95.         if self.entries.len() >= self.capacity {
96.             self.evict();
97.         }
98.     }
99. 
100.     self.counter += 1;
101.     self.entries.insert(key, CacheEntry { value, last_used: self.counter });
102. }
103. ```
104. 
105. This is semantically equivalent to the original: both produce the same `Map<K, V>`
106. contents and the same LRU ordering. The existing VERUS REWRITE precedents in
107. `Cache::remove` (lib.rs:284) and `Cache::evict` (lib.rs:352-354) confirm this
108. pattern is accepted in the codebase.
109. 
110. ### Specific Question
111. 
112. **Rewrite `Cache::put` to avoid `get_mut`, remove `external_body`, and make it verify.**
113. 
114. Specifically:
115. 
116. 1. **Rewrite the body** (lines 238–265) using the remove+insert pattern shown above.
117.    Mark the rewrite with `// VERUS REWRITE: replace get_mut with remove+insert`.
118. 
119. 2. **Remove `#[verus_verify(external_body)]`** from `Cache::put` (line 230).
120. 
121. 3. **Add a new axiom `axiom_cache_lru_of_insert`** in lib.proof.rs (analogous to
122.    `axiom_cache_lru_of_remove`) that captures how `cache_lru_of` changes after
123.    `BTreeMap::insert`. The axiom should state:
124. 
125.    > Inserting a new `CacheEntry` with `last_used` strictly greater than all
126.    > existing entries' `last_used` values appends the key to the end of `cache_lru_of`
127.    > (i.e., makes it the MRU).
128. 
129.    The soundness argument: `cache_lru_of` is "sorted by `last_used` ascending", so
130.    the entry with the highest `last_used` must appear last. Since `self.counter` is
131.    monotonically incremented before every insert, the new entry's `last_used` is
132.    always the largest.
133. 
134.    **Important:** This axiom references `CacheEntry.last_used` (crate-private), which
135.    is appropriate since it's within the crate's trust boundary. The axiom must have a
136.    precondition requiring the inserted entry's `last_used` to be greater than all
137.    existing entries' `last_used`, since we can express this via the entries map.
138. 
139. 4. **Add a proof lemma `lemma_put_view`** proving the postconditions for all branches:
140.    - Zero-capacity: no-op, trivial
141.    - Key existed (remove returned Some): `remove(key).insert(key, new_value)` matches
142.      `spec_put`'s overwrite case. LRU: `axiom_cache_lru_of_remove` filters out key,
143.      then `axiom_cache_lru_of_insert` appends key — net effect is `move_to_mru`.
144.    - New key at capacity: `evict` + `insert` matches `spec_put`'s eviction case
145.    - New key below capacity: `insert` matches `spec_put`'s simple insert case
146. 
147.    Use `reveal(<Cache<_, _> as View>::view)`, `reveal(cache_contents_of)`,
148.    `reveal(cache_lru_of)`, and the existing invariant lemmas.
149.

# Verus Attribute-Based Syntax — Quick Reference

Use `#[verus_spec]` for exec functions, `verus! {}` for spec/proof functions.

Files in this directory:
- **SKILL.md** — this file, daily-use quick reference
- **GUIDE.md** — advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits)
- **syntax_attr.rs** — official Verus example (from `verus-lang/verus/examples/syntax_attr.rs`)

## When to Use What

| Context | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Exec function specs | `#[verus_spec(...)]` |
| Mark external_body | `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` |
| Loop invariants | `#[verus_spec(invariant ...)]` on loop |
| Proof blocks inside exec | `proof! { ... }` |
| Function-scoped ghost vars | `proof_decl! { ... }` |
| Spec fn / proof fn | `verus! { ... }` (unchanged) |

For advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits),
see `GUIDE.md` in this skill directory.

## #[verus_spec] — Function Specifications

```rust
#[verus_spec(sum =>
    requires
        x < 100,
        y < 100,
    ensures
        sum < 200,
)]
fn my_exec_fun(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
    x + y
}
```

Named return (`sum =>`) binds the return value. Omit if not needed:

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    requires x < 100,
)]
fn do_something(x: u32) { /* ... */ }
```

Bare `#[verus_spec]` marks for verification with no specs:

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn simple_function() { /* verified, no contracts */ }
```

Supported clauses: `requires`, `ensures`, `decreases`, `returns`, `with`.

## #[verus_verify] — Verification Hints

```rust
#[verus_verify]                    // mark for verification
#[verus_verify(external_body)]     // skip body verification
#[verus_verify(external)]          // skip entirely
#[verus_verify(rlimit(50))]        // resource limit
```

Combine with `#[verus_spec]`:

```rust
#[verus_verify(external_body)]
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x > 0,
    ensures ret == x,
)]
fn wrapper(x: u32) -> u32 { x }
```

## Loop Invariants

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant
        v@ =~= Seq::new(i as nat, |k| k as u32),
)]
for i in 0..n {
    v.push(i);
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
)]
while i < 10 {
    i = i + 1;
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
    invariant_except_break i <= 9,
    ensures i == 10, ret == 10,
)]
loop {
    i = i + 1;
    if i == 10 { ret = i; break; }
}
```

## proof! { } — Proof Blocks

Block-scoped proof code inside exec functions:

```rust
#[verus_spec(requires x < 100, y < 100)]
fn test(x: u32, y: u32) {
    proof! {
        let u = my_spec_fun(x as int, y as int);
        my_proof_fun(u / 2, y as int);
        assert(f1(3) > 3) by { reveal(f1); };
        assert(x ^ x == 0u32) by (bit_vector);
    }
}
```

## proof_decl! { } — Function-Scoped Ghost Variables

Variables persist across the entire function (not just one block):

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn test() {
    proof_decl! {
        let ghost mut x;
        let tracked y = false;
        x = 2int;
    }
    some_exec_call();
    proof! {
        assert(x == 2);  // still in scope
        assert(!y);
    }
}
```

Only `ghost` and `tracked` declarations allowed — no exec `let`, no exec calls.

## Spec/Proof Functions (verus! { })

```rust
verus! {

pub open spec fn is_valid(x: int) -> bool {
    x >= 0 && x < 100
}

proof fn lemma_validity(x: int)
    requires is_valid(x),
    ensures x + 1 < 101,
{}

} // verus!
```

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or
about `&mut` complex args), not about closures. You must isolate and test
the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

### Required diagnostic steps

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.
   - If a closure-taking function fails, test a standalone closure first,
     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement
6. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — follow the escalation ladder in Source
   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.
7. **Stdlib wrapper** — only after isolated repro shows the API call itself
   is the failing unit (see Source Integrity step 4).

### Examples of past false generalizations

| Error on | False conclusion | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `v.partition_point(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `partition_point` lacks vstd spec; closures work fine |
| `v.sort_by_key(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `&mut` complex args unsupported; closures work fine |
| `for x in v.windows(2)` | "iterators not supported" | `Windows` lacks `ForLoopGhostIteratorNew`; `for x in vec` works |
| `for i in (0..n).rev()` | "ranges not supported" | `Rev<Range>` lacks trait impl; `for i in 0..n` works |
| `x.ok_or_else(\|\| err)` | "closures not supported" | Works — vstd has `assume_specification` for it |

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept — or use
`external_body` and document in trust.md.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.

1. # Verus Attribute Syntax — Advanced Guide
2. 
3. Companion to `SKILL.md`. Covers patterns needed less frequently.
4. See also `syntax_attr.rs` in this directory for the official Verus example.
5. 
6. ---
7. 
8. ## Ghost/Tracked Parameters (`with` clause)
9. 
10. Functions can accept ghost/tracked parameters invisible to non-Verus callers.
11. 
12. ### Declaring a function with ghost/tracked params
13. 
14. ```rust
15. #[verus_spec(ret =>
16.     with
17.         Tracked(y): Tracked<&mut u32>,
18.         Ghost(w): Ghost<u64>
19.             -> z: Ghost<u32>
20.     requires
21.         x < 100,
22.         *old(y) < 100,
23.     ensures
24.         *y == x,
25.         ret == x,
26.         z == x,
27. )]
28. fn test_mut_tracked(x: u32) -> u32 {
29.     proof!{ *y = x; }
30.     #[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]
31.     x
32. }
33. ```
34. 
35. - The `with` clause declares ghost/tracked inputs and ghost outputs (`-> z: Ghost<u32>`).
36. - `#[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]` on the return expression returns a ghost output.
37. 
38. ### Calling with ghost/tracked
39. 
40. Use `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` on the call expression:
41. 
42. ```rust
43. fn test_cal_mut_tracked(x: u32) {
44.     proof_decl!{
45.         let ghost mut z;
46.         let tracked mut y = 0u32;
47.         z = 0u32;
48.     }
49. 
50.     // On a let statement:
51.     #[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0) => Ghost(z))]
52.     let _ = test_mut_tracked(0u32);
53. 
54.     // On a bare expression (wrap in parens):
55.     (#[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0))]
56.     test_mut_tracked(0u32));
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. ### How it works
61. 
62. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` generates **two versions** of the function:
63. - A verified version (`_VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`) with ghost/tracked parameters
64. - An unverified version (original signature) with `requires false`
65. 
66. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` at the call site calls the verified version.
67. Without it, the unverified version is called — which has `requires false`,
68. so calling from verified code without the `with` annotation will fail.
69. 
70. Unverified code can call the original version normally:
71. 
72. ```rust
73. fn external_caller(x: u32) -> u32 {
74.     test_mut_tracked(1)  // calls unverified version, no with needed
75. }
76. ```
77. 
78. ### Compatibility limitation
79. 
80. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` call-site syntax only works with exec functions
81. verified via `#[verus_spec]`. Using it to call an exec function defined
82. inside `verus! { }` will error: `cannot find function _VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`.
83. 
84. Workaround: create a trusted wrapper:
85. 
86. ```rust
87. #[verus_verify(external_body)]
88. #[verus_spec(v =>
89.     with Tracked(perm): Tracked<&mut PointsTo<T>>
90.     requires
91.         old(perm).ptr() == ptr,
92.         old(perm).is_init(),
93.     ensures
94.         perm.ptr() == ptr,
95.         perm.is_uninit(),
96.         v == old(perm).value(),
97. )]
98. fn ptr_mut_read<'a, T>(ptr: *const T) -> T {
99.     vstd::raw_ptr::ptr_mut_read(ptr, Tracked::assume_new())
100. }
101. ```
102. 
103. ---
104. 
105. ## Dual-Mode Functions (exec → spec)
106. 
107. Automatically generate a spec mirror of an exec function:
108. 
109. ```rust
110. #[verus_verify(dual_spec(spec_add))]
111. #[verus_spec(
112.     requires x < 100, y < 100,
113.     returns add(x, y),
114. )]
115. fn add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
116.     proof! { assert(true); }
117.     x + y
118. }
119. // Generates: spec fn spec_add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 { x + y }
120. // Proof/ghost code is stripped from the generated spec function
121. ```
122. 
123. Without a custom name, an internal name `__VERUS_SPEC_xxx` is generated.
124. The `#[when_used_as_spec]` attribute lets you use the exec name as a spec:
125. 
126. ```rust
127. #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
128. #[verus_spec(
129.     requires x < 100,
130.     returns f2(x),
131. )]
132. pub fn f2(x: u32) -> u32 {
133.     add(x, 1)
134. }
135. // Use f2(x) directly in spec context — resolves to __VERUS_SPEC_f2(x)
136. ```
137. 
138. Works on impl methods too:
139. 
140. ```rust
141. impl S {
142.     #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
143.     #[verus_spec(
144.         returns self.foo(x),
145.     )]
146.     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32 { x }
147. }
148. ```
149. 
150. **Limitations:**
151. - Requires `#[verus_spec]` — does not work with `verus!` macro
152. - `&mut` parameters are not supported (spec functions cannot take `&mut`)
153. - Not supported on trait implementations (error: "method `spec_f` is not
154.   a member of trait")
155. 
156. ---
157. 
158. ## Trait Function Specs
159. 
160. ```rust
161. trait MyTrait {
162.     #[verus_spec(r =>
163.         requires
164.             0 <= i < 10,
165.             0 <= j < 10,
166.         ensures
167.             i <= r,
168.             j <= r,
169.     )]
170.     fn compute(&self, i: u8, j: u8) -> u8;
171. }
172. ```
173. 
174. Default trait implementations:
175. 
176. ```rust
177. #[verus_verify]
178. trait SomeTrait {
179.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
180.         requires true,
181.         ensures ret,
182.     )]
183.     fn f(&self) -> bool {
184.         true
185.     }
186. }
187. ```
188. 
189. **Limitation:** `with` (ghost/tracked parameters) is not supported on
190. trait methods — error: "`with` does not support trait".
191. 
192. ---
193. 
194. ## Closure Specs
195. 
196. ```rust
197. let f =
198.     #[verus_spec(z: u64 =>
199.         requires y == 2,
200.         ensures z == 2,
201.     )]
202.     |y: u64| { y };
203. 
204. proof! {
205.     assert(f.requires((2,)));
206.     assert(!f.ensures((2,), 3));
207. }
208. let t = f(2);
209. proof! { assert(t == 2); }
210. ```
211. 
212. **Note:** Closures must have a return type annotation or a named return
213. in the spec. A closure with no return type and no named return will error:
214. "Closure must have a return type". Use either `|y: u64| -> () { }` or
215. `#[verus_spec(ret: () => ...)]`.
216. 
217. ---
218. 
219. ## Const Functions
220. 
221. ```rust
222. #[verus_spec(ret =>
223.     ensures ret == x,
224. )]
225. pub const fn identity(x: u64) -> u64 {
226.     proof! { assert(true); }
227.     x
228. }
229. 
230. pub const X: u64 = identity(1);
231. ```
232. 
233. ---
234. 
235. ## Macros Inside Proof Blocks
236. 
237. Rust macros can be used inside `proof_decl!`:
238. 
239. ```rust
240. macro_rules! inline_proof {
241.     ($val:expr => $x:ident, $y:ident) => {
242.         proof_decl! {
243.             let tracked $x: int = $val;
244.             let ghost $y: int = $val;
245.             assert($x == $y);
246.         }
247.     }
248. }
249. 
250. fn test() {
251.     proof_decl! {
252.         inline_proof!(0 => x, y);
253.         assert(x == 0);
254.     }
255. }
256. ```
257. 
258. ---
259. 
260. ## Known Limitations Summary
261. 
262. | Feature | Status |
263. |---|---|
264. | `with` call-site + `verus!{}` fn | ✗ — wrap in attribute-style fn |

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or
about `&mut` complex args), not about closures. You must isolate and test
the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

### Required diagnostic steps

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.
   - If a closure-taking function fails, test a standalone closure first,
     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement
6. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — follow the escalation ladder in Source
   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.
7. **Stdlib wrapper** — only after isolated repro shows the API call itself
   is the failing unit (see Source Integrity step 4).

### Examples of past false generalizations

| Error on | False conclusion | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `v.partition_point(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `partition_point` lacks vstd spec; closures work fine |
| `v.sort_by_key(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `&mut` complex args unsupported; closures work fine |
| `for x in v.windows(2)` | "iterators not supported" | `Windows` lacks `ForLoopGhostIteratorNew`; `for x in vec` works |
| `for i in (0..n).rev()` | "ranges not supported" | `Rev<Range>` lacks trait impl; `for i in 0..n` works |
| `x.ok_or_else(\|\| err)` | "closures not supported" | Works — vstd has `assume_specification` for it |

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept — or use
`external_body` and document in trust.md.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.

name: review-methodology
description: "Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks."

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code (use `detect_cheating` tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

4. //! Bounded LRU cache backed by `BTreeMap`.
5. //!
6. //! Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by a caller-chosen type `K` that
7. //! implements `Ord + Clone`. A monotonic counter tracks access order; on
8. //! eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed.
9. //! Lookups bump the counter to mark the entry as recently used.
10. //!
11. //! # Capacity
12. //!
13. //! The cache is bounded by a capacity given at construction time. When the
14. //! cache is full, the least-recently-used entry is evicted before inserting a
15. //! new one.
16. //!
17. //! # Example
18. //!
19. //! ```
20. //! use cache::Cache;
21. //!
22. //! let mut cache: Cache<&str, i32> = Cache::new(2);
23. //! cache.put("a", 1);
24. //! cache.put("b", 2);
25. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"a").unwrap(), 1);
26. //!
27. //! // Inserting a third entry evicts "b" (least recently used).
28. //! cache.put("c", 3);
29. //! assert!(cache.get(&"b").is_none());
30. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"c").unwrap(), 3);
31. //! ```
32. 
33. #![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
34. #![cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, feature(proc_macro_hygiene))]
35. #![cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, feature(allocator_api))]

62. /// A single entry in the cache.
63. #[derive(Clone)]
64. struct CacheEntry<V> {
65.     /// Cached value.
66.     value: V,
67.     /// Last-access counter (higher = more recently used).

69. }

75. ///
76. /// # Description
77. ///
78. /// RAII guard providing a reference to a cached entry.
79. ///
80. /// Created by [`Cache::get()`]. Dereferences to `&V` for read access
81. /// and `&mut V` for write access. The LRU counter is bumped when the guard
82. /// is created.
83. ///
84. pub struct CacheGuard<'a, V> {
85.     /// Mutable reference to the cached value.
86.     value: &'a mut V,
87. }

129. ///
130. /// # Description
131. ///
132. /// A bounded cache using access-counter LRU approximation.
133. ///
134. /// Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by `K`. A monotonic counter tracks access order;
135. /// on eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed. Lookups bump the
136. /// counter to mark the entry as recently used.
137. ///
138. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(K))]
139. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(V))]
140. pub struct Cache<K, V> {
141.     /// Cached entries.
142.     entries: BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
143.     /// Monotonically increasing counter for LRU ordering.
144.     counter: u64,
145.     /// Maximum number of entries.
146.     capacity: usize,
147. }

151.     ///
152.     /// # Description
153.     ///
154.     /// Creates a new empty cache with the given capacity.
155.     ///
156.     /// # Parameters
157.     ///
158.     /// - `capacity`: Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
159.     ///
160.     #[verus_spec(result =>
161.         ensures
162.             result@ == CacheView::<K, V>::spec_new(capacity as nat),
163.             result@.inv(),
164.     )]
165.     pub const fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
166.         let result = Self {
167.             entries: BTreeMap::new(),
168.             counter: 0,
169.             capacity,
170.         };
171.         proof! {
172.             Self::lemma_new_view(&result, capacity);
173.         }
174.         result
175.     }

177.     ///
178.     /// # Description
179.     ///
180.     /// Looks up a cached value and bumps its LRU counter on hit.
181.     ///
182.     /// # Parameters
183.     ///
184.     /// - `key`: The cache key to look up.
185.     ///
186.     /// # Returns
187.     ///
188.     /// An RAII guard providing access to the cached value, or `None` on cache miss.

200.                 &&& self@.inv()

202.             // Miss: key is absent.
203.             !old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> {
204.                 &&& result is None
205.                 &&& self@ == old(self)@

207.     )]
208.     pub fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<CacheGuard<'_, V>> {
209.         if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(key) {
210.             self.counter += 1;
211.             entry.last_used = self.counter;
212.             Some(CacheGuard {
213.                 value: &mut entry.value,
214.             })
215.         } else {
216.             None
217.         }
218.     }

220.     ///
221.     /// # Description
222.     ///
223.     /// Inserts a value, evicting the least-recently-used entry if at capacity.
224.     ///
225.     /// # Parameters
226.     ///
227.     /// - `key`: The cache key to insert or update.
228.     /// - `value`: The value to store.
229.     ///
230.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
231.     #[verus_spec(
232.         requires
233.             old(self)@.inv(),
234.         ensures
235.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value),
236.             self@.inv(),
237.     )]
238.     pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
239.         // A zero-capacity cache cannot store entries.
240.         if self.capacity == 0 {
241.             return;
242.         }
243. 
244.         // If the key is already present, update in place.
245.         if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(&key) {
246.             self.counter += 1;
247.             entry.value = value;
248.             entry.last_used = self.counter;
249.             return;
250.         }
251. 
252.         // Evict the LRU entry if at capacity.
253.         if self.entries.len() >= self.capacity {
254.             self.evict();
255.         }
256. 
257.         self.counter += 1;
258.         self.entries.insert(
259.             key,
260.             CacheEntry {
261.                 value,
262.                 last_used: self.counter,
263.             },
264.         );
265.     }

540. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> Cache<K, V> {
541.     /// Proves that Cache::evict (after extracting find_lru_victim) produces
542.     /// the correct postconditions: the LRU victim is removed, lru_order drops
543.     /// its first element, capacity is preserved, and inv holds.
544.     proof fn lemma_evict_view(
545.         new_self: &Self,
546.         victim: K,
547.         old_entries: alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
548.         old_capacity: usize,
549.     )
550.         requires
551.             // victim is the LRU key
552.             cache_lru_of(old_entries).len() > 0,
553.             victim == cache_lru_of(old_entries)[0],
554.             // entries after btreemap_remove
555.             btreemap_view_spec(new_self.entries) == btreemap_view_spec(old_entries).remove(victim),
556.             new_self.capacity == old_capacity,
557.             // Old state was well-formed (inv fields via abstraction helpers)
558.             cache_contents_of(old_entries).dom().len() <= old_capacity as nat,
559.             cache_lru_of(old_entries).no_duplicates(),
560.             cache_lru_of(old_entries).to_set() == cache_contents_of(old_entries).dom(),
561.             cache_lru_of(old_entries).len() == cache_contents_of(old_entries).dom().len(),
562.         ensures
563.             new_self@.contents == cache_contents_of(old_entries).remove(victim),
564.             !new_self@.contents.dom().contains(victim),
565.             new_self@.contents.dom().len() == cache_contents_of(old_entries).dom().len() - 1,
566.             new_self@.lru_order == cache_lru_of(old_entries).subrange(
567.                 1, cache_lru_of(old_entries).len() as int,
568.             ),
569.             new_self@.capacity == old_capacity as nat,
570.             new_self@.inv(),
571.     {
572.         broadcast use vstd::set::group_set_axioms, vstd::map::group_map_axioms,
573.             vstd::seq_lib::seq_to_set_is_finite;
574. 
575.         reveal(<Cache<_, _> as View>::view);
576.         reveal(cache_contents_of);
577.         reveal(cache_lru_of);
578. 
579.         let old_lru = cache_lru_of(old_entries);
580. 
581.         // Apply LRU axiom: removing victim from entries filters the LRU order.
582.         axiom_cache_lru_of_remove(old_entries, new_self.entries, victim);
583.         // Now: cache_lru_of(new_self.entries) == old_lru.filter(|k| k != victim)
584. 
585.         // Key insight: filter(|k| k != s[0]) == subrange(1, len) for no-dup sequences.
586.         lemma_filter_first_is_subrange(old_lru);
587. 
588.         // Invariant properties for the new state:
589.         // 1. no_duplicates for the subranged lru_order
590.         lemma_subrange_no_dup(old_lru, 1, old_lru.len() as int);
591. 
592.         // 2. to_set: subrange(1, len).to_set() == to_set().remove(s[0])
593.         lemma_drop_first_to_set(old_lru);
594. 
595.         // 3. contents: cache_contents_of after remove
596.         assert(new_self@.contents =~= cache_contents_of(old_entries).remove(victim));
597.     }
598. }
599.

data.content:
Main issue I see:

- **Blocking — your new insert axiom is too strong without a freshness precondition.**  
  `cache_lru_of` is specified as keys sorted by `last_used` (`lib.spec.rs:40-50`).  
  So `cache_lru_of(new_entries) == cache_lru_of(old_entries).push(key)` is only valid if the inserted entry’s `last_used` is greater than every existing entry’s `last_used`. Without that, the axiom is not just hard to prove — it is **false** for some concrete maps, which would widen the trust boundary unsafely.  
  **Fix:** either:
  1. add the reviewer’s freshness precondition and the concrete invariant needed to prove it (`forall k in entries: entries[k].last_used <= counter`), or  
  2. keep `put` as `external_body` for now.  
  I would not merge the axiom in its current form.

Other important notes:

- **Blocking — `reveal(Cache::view) + reveal(cache_lru_of)` is not sufficient by itself after `evict()`.**  
  `cache_lru_of` is uninterpreted on nonempty maps, so revealing it does not explain how the final concrete `insert` changes LRU order. You still need an explicit concrete-map relation for the post-insert state (i.e. your insert axiom/lemma).  
  **Fix:** plan the final proof around:
  - `evict()`’s abstract ensures for the pre-insert abstract state, and
  - a concrete post-insert step from `btreemap_view_spec(pre_insert_entries).insert(...)` to the final `self@`.

- **Non-blocking but likely proof blocker — absent-key remove equalities probably won’t be automatic.**  
  I would not assume Verus derives `map.remove(absent) =~= map` on its own. Same for “remove absent leaves `cache_contents_of` unchanged.”  
  **Fix:** expect to add explicit extensional assertions / helper lemmas for:
  - `m.remove(k) =~= m` when `k ∉ dom(m)`
  - `cache_contents_of(entries_after_absent_remove) =~= cache_contents_of(old_entries)`

- **Non-blocking — don’t depend on `ghost mut` unless you’ve confirmed the syntax works here.**  
  In this codebase, snapshots are typically immutable ghost locals (`let ghost old_self = *self;`). Since you only need a snapshot of the pre-insert map, `mut` seems unnecessary and may become a side issue.  
  **Fix:** prefer a single immutable ghost snapshot of the pre-insert concrete state.

One positive point:

- The **remove+insert runtime rewrite itself looks semantically right** for `spec_put`; the risky part is the **new trusted LRU axiom**, not the exec code shape.

So my recommendation is: **treat the missing `last_used` precondition as a blocker**. If you can’t afford the concrete invariant work now, keeping `put` as `external_body` is safer than adding an underconstrained axiom.

397. // Axiom: removing a key from entries produces the old LRU ordering filtered to
398. // exclude that key. Sound because BTreeMap::remove doesn't change last_used
399. // counters of remaining entries, so their relative sort order is preserved.
400. // Trust boundary: documented in trust.md.
401. #[verifier::external_body]
402. proof fn axiom_cache_lru_of_remove<K, V>(
403.     old_entries: alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
404.     new_entries: alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
405.     key: K,
406. )
407.     requires
408.         btreemap_view_spec(new_entries) == btreemap_view_spec(old_entries).remove(key),
409.     ensures
410.         cache_lru_of(new_entries) == cache_lru_of(old_entries).filter(|k: K| k != key),
411. {}

+// Axiom: inserting a new key-entry pair into entries appends the key at the
+// end of the LRU order. Sound because BTreeMap::insert for a new key does not
+// change last_used counters of existing entries, and the new entry (with the
+// highest counter value due to monotonic incrementing) sorts last.
+// Trust boundary: documented in trust.md.
+#[verifier::external_body]
+proof fn axiom_cache_lru_of_insert<K, V>(
+    old_entries: alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
+    new_entries: alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
+    key: K,
+    entry: CacheEntry<V>,
+)
+    requires
+        !btreemap_view_spec(old_entries).dom().contains(key),
+        btreemap_view_spec(new_entries) == btreemap_view_spec(old_entries).insert(key, entry),
+    ensures
+        cache_lru_of(new_entries) == cache_lru_of(old_entries).push(key),
+{}
+
 //==================================================================================================
 // Cache::remove Verification Lemma
 //==================================================================================================
